# RFC-0004: Host capabilities, portability and caching

> **Version:** 0.1.0 | **Status:** draft | **Phase:** spec
> **Owners:** @wael
> **Tags:** `architecture`, `out-of-core`

---

## 1. Summary

### [RFC-0004:C-OVERVIEW] Overview and scope (Informative) <a id="rfc-0004c-overview"></a>

A library crate reaches for nothing. Storage, byte retrieval and parallelism arrive from whoever is
hosting it, and everything derived from them — caches, spilled working sets, consolidated overlays —
inherits the same discipline. Two consequences follow that would otherwise be separate subjects: the
same code runs in a desktop process and in a browser, and a cache cannot acquire authority it was never
given.

**Scope** — how library crates obtain environment capabilities rather than assuming them; the
prohibition on blocking; the checks that keep that honest; and how derived artefacts are layered, keyed
and integrity-checked.

**Out of scope** — a browser or server deployment, neither of which is being built. Rendering backends
([RFC-0006:C-SURFACE](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-surface)). Cache eviction policy, sizing and placement heuristics. The concrete storage
and retrieval implementations, which are the host's.

Two points deserve stating because both are easy to lose. First, the distinction between an aspiration
and an obligation: intending to stay portable does not survive a deadline, so C-PORT-GATE makes it a
check that fails. Second, this RFC introduces **no virtual filesystem** — paths, directory traversal,
seekable handles and permissions are all more privilege than any of this needs. A keyed store with no
paths has no path traversal to defend against, and a write-once store has no in-place modification to
race. That narrowness is the security property, and widening these interfaces toward a general
filesystem would forfeit it.

---

## 2. Specification

### [RFC-0004:C-HOST] Host-supplied capabilities (Normative) <a id="rfc-0004c-host"></a>

Capability interfaces are shaped by the **weakest plausible backend**, not the most convenient one.
Browser-resident storage is a keyed store with no directories and no in-place modification; object stores
share the second property; a browser page has threads only under conditions frequently unavailable, and its
main thread cannot block. An interface assuming otherwise works on the desktop and fails everywhere else —
as a redesign, not a port.

1. A library crate MUST obtain persistent byte storage through a storage interface supplied by its caller,
   and MUST NOT call filesystem APIs directly.
   - This covers any spill, cache, or temporary working set ([RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 7).
   - The interface MUST NOT assume hierarchical paths.
   - The interface MUST NOT assume a stored item can be modified in place after being written.
2. A library crate MUST obtain byte ranges through a retrieval interface supplied by its caller.
   - Every read MUST be expressed as an explicit offset and length, not against a seekable handle.
   - The interface MUST support requesting several ranges as one operation.
3. A library crate MUST obtain parallelism from an executor supplied by its caller, and MUST NOT spawn
   operating-system threads directly.
   - It MUST remain functionally correct when that executor runs all work on a single thread, differing
     only in throughput.
4. A library crate MUST NOT block its calling thread awaiting retrieval, storage, or computation.

#### Rationale

Which store is available is the caller's knowledge, not the library's: a filesystem on the desktop, an
object store on a server, a keyed store in a page.

Explicit offset and length in (2), rather than a seekable stream, is what makes the interface implementable
where retrieval is request-shaped rather than handle-shaped, and what lets an implementation serve a read
from cache without a round trip. Batched multi-range requests are required because the access pattern
demands them: resolving a viewport typically names on the order of a hundred nodes at once, and issuing
those sequentially over a network multiplies latency by the node count — the difference between a viewport
that fills promptly and one that visibly trickles.

Single-threaded correctness in (3) is the substantive half of that requirement, not a portability
concession. It makes every operator deterministically testable without a thread pool, turns a class of
concurrency bug into a reproducible failure, and means the single-threaded configuration is a real fallback
rather than an untested path. An algorithm that is only correct when work is genuinely concurrent has a
defect this surfaces immediately.

(4) is likewise independently required on the desktop: [RFC-0006:C-RENDER](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-render) 2 obliges rendering requests
to be cancellable without draining dispatched work, and a blocked thread cannot observe a cancellation.

One cost is worth naming at the obligation rather than leaving to the decision record: memory-mapped I/O
cannot be expressed through (2) at all. What that forfeits, and where it may be recovered, is argued in the
accompanying architecture decision.

### [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE] Portability enforcement (Normative) <a id="rfc-0004c-port-gate"></a>

This clause is what makes C-HOST real. A codebase written with portability in mind but never compiled for a
constrained target is portable for about three weeks. One gate is not enough, because the obvious one does
not catch the obvious violation.

1. Every library crate MUST compile for a target that provides no filesystem access, no threads, and no
   blocking I/O.
2. Every library crate MUST additionally pass a lint that rejects references to ambient capabilities.
   - The lint MUST reject filesystem types and calls, thread spawning, and sleeping.
3. Both checks MUST run on every change, and a failure of either MUST be treated as a defect rather than as
   an unsupported configuration.
4. A library crate MUST NOT contain environment-specific code paths.

#### Rationale

(2) exists because (1) alone is insufficient — a constrained target's standard library may *stub* the very
capabilities it lacks, so code referencing them compiles and fails only at run time. The two checks catch
different classes: the target catches a dependency that cannot build at all, the lint catches a call the
stub would accept. Neither substitutes for the other. The measurement establishing this, and why intent was
judged inadequate, are in the accompanying architecture decision.

Running on *every* change rather than periodically (3) is the operative part. A portability check run
occasionally accumulates a backlog that is then cheaper to declare unsupported than to fix, which is the
outcome this clause exists to prevent.

(4) is what keeps (1) and (2) from being satisfied trivially by conditional compilation. The residual risk
neither check closes is a capability interface acquiring a method only a filesystem can implement — that
would satisfy both and defeat the purpose, and it is accepted as the price of cheap gates rather than
hidden. Enforcement is compile-time and lint-time only; a browser test suite and a browser deployment are
out of scope per C-OVERVIEW.

### [RFC-0004:C-CACHE] Cache layering and keying (Normative) <a id="rfc-0004c-cache"></a>

A cache is a derived artefact and never a source of truth. Everything below follows from that, plus the
observation that the host interfaces already provide everything a cache needs — so nothing here widens the
privilege a library crate holds.

1. A cache MUST NOT be authoritative.
   - Every cache entry MUST be re-derivable from authoritative state and discardable at any time without
     loss. This generalises [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake) 4 from the consolidated edit overlay to every cache.
2. A cache MUST obtain its persistence through the storage interface and its inputs through the retrieval
   interface (C-HOST 1 and 2).
   - It MUST NOT require a hierarchical namespace or path traversal.
   - It MUST NOT require seekable handles.
   - It MUST NOT require in-place modification of a stored entry.
3. A cache of byte ranges MUST be an implementation of the retrieval interface rather than a separate
   concept.
   - A caching and a non-caching source MUST be interchangeable to their consumer.
4. A cache of decoded batches MUST be keyed per attribute.
   - It MUST NOT be keyed on the projection requested by any particular consumer.

#### Rationale

(2) enumerates four separate prohibitions rather than stating "use the host interfaces", because each names a
capability a cache implementation would plausibly reach for and each is independently checkable. Why the
narrow surface is preferable to a filesystem abstraction is a comparative question, argued in the
accompanying architecture decision rather than here.

(3) follows from C-HOST 2's shape: retrieval defined as explicit offset and length makes a cache an
implementation of that interface rather than a layer beside it, so coalescing logic stays portable while the
backing store remains the host's.

(4) exists because [RFC-0002:C-PROJECTION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-projection) would otherwise force a choice between fragmenting the cache per
distinct projection and caching whole records, which discards the benefit projection exists for. Per-attribute
keying avoids both; why that beats the alternatives is in the accompanying architecture decision.

Fingerprint recording is not restated here: [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) 5 already requires every derived artefact
to carry the source version it was built from, and a cache entry is one.

### [RFC-0004:C-INTEGRITY] Cache integrity (Normative) <a id="rfc-0004c-integrity"></a>

[RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) 5 detects a *stale* cache entry, not a *modified* one. A cache held in shared storage
can be altered by something other than this software, and the consequence is not uniform: a tampered baked
overlay would change a delivered result while [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake) 2 asserts that baking cannot change
results.

1. Every cache entry MUST carry a digest of its own content.
2. A cache entry contributing to a committed run ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit)) MUST be verified against its digest
   before use.
3. Failed verification MUST result in the entry being discarded and re-derived.
   - It MUST NOT interrupt the operation or be surfaced as an error to the user.
   - Where the entry was contributing to a committed run, the failure MUST be recorded in that run's
     evaluation configuration ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 4).
   - Repeated verification failure for the same key MUST terminate rather than re-derive indefinitely, and
     MUST be reported when it does.
4. A cache entry used only for preview or rendering MAY be used without verification.

#### Rationale

(2) and (4) draw the verification boundary at the committed path rather than at every read. Why that is the
right boundary — what the interactive path costs, and what a preview is permitted to be wrong about — is
argued in the accompanying architecture decision.

The first sub-item of (3) is what makes this cheap rather than fragile. C-CACHE 1 guarantees every entry is
re-derivable, so a verification failure degrades to a cache miss; treating it as an error would convert a
recoverable condition into an interruption, and would tempt an implementation to skip verification to avoid
spurious failures.

The second and third sub-items exist because silence and recoverability are different things. Discarding
quietly is right for the *operation*; discarding quietly and leaving no trace anywhere is not, because the
threat model here includes tampering, and a delivered result whose inputs were repeatedly found corrupt
should say so. Recording it in the evaluation configuration costs nothing — [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 4 already
requires that record to exist. And an unbounded discard-and-re-derive loop against a persistent corrupting
agent is a hang, not a mitigation, so termination is required and is the one case that does surface.

The obligation overall is detection, not prevention. Nothing here stops an entry from being altered; the
guarantee is that an altered entry cannot silently contribute to a delivered result.
